solution:
Magnetic flux **linkage** is \(N\Phi\), not the flux \(\Phi\) through one turn — that distinction is the whole point of the question.

Flux through a single turn, with the field normal to the coil face \((\theta = 0^\circ)\):

\(\Phi = BA\cos\theta = (1\ \text{T})(1\ \text{m}^2)(1) = 1\) Wb

Flux linkage with all 100 turns:

\(N\Phi = 100 \times 1 = 100\) Wb

Why the others fail: 1 Wb is the flux through **one** turn — the answer you get by forgetting that the coil has 100 turns. 50 Wb would need an extra factor of \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) (or \(\cos 60^\circ\)), which nothing in the data supplies. 200 Wb is twice the linkage.

A note on the wording: taken literally, "plane perpendicular to the magnetic field" would put \(\vec{B}\) **in** the plane of the coil and give \(\Phi = 0\), which is not among the options. The book uses this phrase throughout to mean the field is perpendicular to the plane, i.e. along the area vector — the same sense as in Example 12.1 of this chapter.

A rod of length \(l\) translating with velocity \(\vec{\mathrm{v}}\) sweeps out area at the rate \(l\mathrm{v}\). With \(\vec{B}\), \(\vec{l}\) and \(\vec{\mathrm{v}}\) mutually perpendicular, the flux swept per second is \(Bl\mathrm{v}\), so

\(|e| = \left| \dfrac{\mathrm{d}\phi}{\mathrm{d}t} \right| = Bl\mathrm{v}\)

Equivalently, the magnetic force on a free electron in the rod is \(q(\vec{\mathrm{v}} \times \vec{B})\), of magnitude \(q\mathrm{v}B\) since the two vectors are perpendicular; charge piles up at the ends until the electrostatic force \(qE\) balances it, giving \(E = \mathrm{v}B\) and a potential difference \(El = Bl\mathrm{v}\).

Why the others fail: \(Bl\mathrm{v}^2\) and \(2Bl/\mathrm{v}\) are not voltages at all — the first carries an extra factor of speed and the second divides by speed, so neither reduces to \(\text{T}\cdot\text{m}\cdot\text{m\,s}^{-1} = \text{V}\). The option \(\tfrac{1}{2}Bl\mathrm{v}\) has the right dimensions but the wrong factor: the \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) belongs to a rod **rotating** about one end, where the ends move at different speeds and only the mean speed \(\omega l/2\) counts. Here the whole rod translates at the same \(\mathrm{v}\).

The condition matters: had \(\vec{\mathrm{v}}\) not been normal to \(\vec{B}\), the emf would be \(Bl\mathrm{v}\sin\theta\). The stem supplies the perpendicularity explicitly.

Inductances in **series** add, exactly as resistances do (assuming no mutual coupling between the two coils):

\(L_{\text{total}} = L_1 + L_2 = 10 + 20 = 30\) mH

Why the others fail: \(\tfrac{20}{3}\) mH is precisely the **parallel** combination, \(\dfrac{L_1 L_2}{L_1 + L_2} = \dfrac{10 \times 20}{30} = \dfrac{20}{3}\) mH — the trap this question is built around. The remaining two options, 20 mH and 10 mH, merely repeat one of the two given values, and in any case a series combination must exceed **both**, so neither can be right on inspection.

For a self-inductance \(L\), the magnitude of the induced (back) emf is

\(|e| = L \left| \dfrac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t} \right|\)

\(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t} = \dfrac{1 - 0}{0.1} = 10\) A/s

\(|e| = (10 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{H})(10\ \text{A/s}) = 0.1\) V

By Lenz's law the emf **opposes** the increase, so it acts against the applied source; only its magnitude is asked for here.

Why the others fail: 1 V is what you get by reading the inductance as 10 H instead of 10 mH; 10 V is 100 times too large; and 0.01 V is \(L \times \Delta i\) with the division by \(\Delta t\) omitted.

The energy stored in the magnetic field of an inductor carrying a steady current \(i\) is

\(U_B = \dfrac{1}{2} L i^2\)

\(= \dfrac{1}{2} (20 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{H})(1\ \text{A})^2 = 10 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{J} = 10\) mJ

Why the others fail: 20 mJ is \(Li^2\) with the factor \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) dropped. The two joule-valued options, 20 J and 10 J, are the same two numbers with the milli- prefix lost — a factor of 1000 too large, which is what makes reading the unit on the answer as important as the arithmetic.
